title: Frederick Douglass (1818–1895) — The Stolen Alphabet, Edward Covey's Barnyard, the Corinthian Hall Thunder, and Confronting Lincoln

teenKit.tldr: Frederick Douglass weaponized literacy, sheer psychological grit, and a borrowed sailor's protection pass to escape slavery and become America’s most feared and brilliant voice for human rights.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It proves that true systemic power is broken not by compliance, but by mastering the tools of communication, refusing to be intimidated, and demanding absolute human dignity.
keyTakeaways: Literacy was treated as a deadly threat by slaveholders because learning to read unlocked the realization of natural rights and the pathways to freedom.

Douglass's grueling two-hour physical showdown with the notorious slave-breaker Edward Covey marked the psychological turning point where he permanently reclaimed his manhood and refused to be subjugated.
Escaping on a moving train with mismatched identity papers required incredible theatrical nerve, psychological dominance, and split-second situational awareness.
